items.title: For a field k and integer n>0, n·1_k is invertible if and only if char(k) does not divide n; 0 divides no positive integer.
items.statement: For a field k and integer n>0, n·1_k is invertible if and only if char(k) does not divide n; 0 divides no positive integer.
items.proof_route: Apply the exact equivalence n·1_k=0 iff char(k)|n in the characteristic lemma, then the field inverse axiom; zero cannot be invertible in a nonzero field.

references.title: Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory
J. S. Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, v5.10 (2022)

items.title: If V is a finite-dimensional k-vector space and U is a subspace, there exists a k-linear P:V→V with P²=P, image P=U and P restricted to U equal to the identity. This uses no choice axiom, including when U=0 or U=V.
items.statement: If V is a finite-dimensional k-vector space and U is a subspace, there exists a k-linear P:V→V with P²=P, image P=U and P restricted to U equal to the identity. This uses no choice axiom, including when U=0 or U=V.
items.proof_route: Use subspace dimension theorem clause 3 first to obtain a finite basis of U and again to extend it to one of V. Keep the U coordinates and zero the added coordinates. Uniqueness of basis coordinates proves well-definedness and linearity. Verify image, restriction and idempotence directly. Only finitely many existential witnesses are used.

references.title: Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory
Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition

items.title: For an idempotent endomorphism P of a finite-dimensional vector space over any field k, tr(P)=(dim_k image P)·1_k. In positive characteristic this is a scalar equality, not recovery of the integer rank from trace.
items.statement: For an idempotent endomorphism P of a finite-dimensional vector space over any field k, tr(P)=(dim_k image P)·1_k. In positive characteristic this is a scalar equality, not recovery of the integer rank from trace.
items.proof_route: The published idempotent corollary supplies V=image P ⊕ kernel P with identity and zero actions. In a basis adapted to that decomposition the matrix is diag(I_r,0). The basis-independent trace is the sum of r copies of 1_k. Include dimension zero.

references.title: Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory
Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition

items.title: For a group acting on a set X with finitely many orbits and any field k, invariant functions X→k form a vector space with basis the indicators of the distinct orbits. The dimension equals the number of orbits. For the conjugation action of a finite group these are class functions and conjugacy-class indicators. The empty X case has the empty basis.
items.statement: For a group acting on a set X with finitely many orbits and any field k, invariant functions X→k form a vector space with basis the indicators of the distinct orbits. The dimension equals the number of orbits. For the conjugation action of a finite group these are class functions and conjugacy-class indicators. The empty X case has the empty basis.
items.proof_route: Check vector-space laws pointwise. An invariant function has a unique value c_O on each nonempty orbit O without choosing representatives, so f=sum_O c_O 1_O pointwise. Evaluation at any member of one orbit proves independence. The conjugation laws follow directly from group associativity and inverses.

references.title: Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory
Thomas W. Judson, Abstract Algebra: Theory and Applications

items.title: For nonempty finite X, the form (f,h)=|X|^(-1) sum_x f(x) conjugate(h(x)) on C^X is an inner product, linear in the first variable. The denominator is the positive real image of |X|.
items.statement: For nonempty finite X, the form (f,h)=|X|^(-1) sum_x f(x) conjugate(h(x)) on C^X is an inner product, linear in the first variable. The denominator is the positive real image of |X|.
items.proof_route: Use finite commutative-monoid sums for complex summands. Prove additivity, complex scaling and conjugation through a finite sum by induction using distributivity and the published conjugation laws. On the diagonal the summands are |f(x)|²; the real finite-sum positivity and zero criterion prove definiteness. Nonempty X makes the normalization strictly positive.

references.title: Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory
Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition

items.title: For n>0 and complex z_1,...,z_n with |z_i|=1, |sum_i z_i|≤n, with equality if and only if all z_i agree. The n=1 case is included.
items.statement: For n>0 and complex z_1,...,z_n with |z_i|=1, |sum_i z_i|≤n, with equality if and only if all z_i agree. The n=1 case is included.
items.proof_route: Expand n²-|sum z_i|²=sum_{i<j}|z_i-z_j|² using finite Fubini, conjugation and distributivity (finite distributivity by induction). Nonnegative real terms yield the inequality after comparison of nonnegative squares. Equality forces every difference to vanish; the converse is direct. No complex argument function or trigonometry is used.

references.title: Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory

items.title: If n>0 and z_1,...,z_n are complex roots of unity and a=(sum_i z_i)/n, then a is algebraic over Q. For every complex Q-conjugate b of a there is a finite cyclotomic splitting field E⊂C containing all z_i and a Q-automorphism σ of E such that b=σ(a)=(sum_i σ(z_i))/n; each σ(z_i) has the same order as z_i. No integrality hypothesis on a is needed.
items.statement: If n>0 and z_1,...,z_n are complex roots of unity and a=(sum_i z_i)/n, then a is algebraic over Q. For every complex Q-conjugate b of a there is a finite cyclotomic splitting field E⊂C containing all z_i and a Q-automorphism σ of E such that b=σ(a)=(sum_i σ(z_i))/n; each σ(z_i) has the same order as z_i. No integrality hypothesis on a is needed.
items.proof_route: Take a positive common multiple N of the finitely many root orders (their product suffices). The complex splitting theorem gives E=Q(μ_N(C))⊂C. It is finite by finite algebraic generation and hence algebraic; its normality follows from the splitting-extension proposition. Thus b lies in E. Simple-root adjunction gives Q(a)≅Q(b), a↦b. E is a splitting field of t^N−1 over each of these intermediate fields, so the splitting-field extension theorem extends this map to an automorphism E→E. It fixes 1/n and preserves each equation z_i^m=1, with inverse preserving exact order. Apply it to the finite sum. This is not an appeal to the one-way assertion that embeddings send elements to conjugates.

references.title: Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory
J. S. Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, v5.10 (2022)

items.title: For a finite family of finite-dimensional k-representations ρ_i of the same group G, the componentwise direct-sum representation has kernel intersection_i ker(ρ_i). For the empty family the representation is on 0 and the intersection is G.
items.statement: For a finite family of finite-dimensional k-representations ρ_i of the same group G, the componentwise direct-sum representation has kernel intersection_i ker(ρ_i). For the empty family the representation is on 0 and the intersection is G.
items.proof_route: Construct the finite direct sum with coordinatewise action; identity, multiplication, linearity and invertibility are coordinatewise (inverse action g^(-1)). An element g acts identically on the sum exactly when it acts identically on each coordinate, tested using coordinate inclusions. Deal with the zero sum separately.

references.title: Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory

items.title: A group G is abelian if and only if every conjugacy class is a singleton; no finiteness hypothesis is required.
items.statement: A group G is abelian if and only if every conjugacy class is a singleton; no finiteness hypothesis is required.
items.proof_route: If gh=hg, then ghg^(-1)=h. Conversely singleton classes give ghg^(-1)=h for every g,h, and right multiplication by g gives gh=hg.

references.title: Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory
Thomas W. Judson, Abstract Algebra: Theory and Applications

items.title: On C³, U=span((1,1,0),(0,1,1)); P(x,y,z)=(x,x+z,z) projects onto U along span((0,1,0)).
items.statement: On C³, U=span((1,1,0),(0,1,1)); P(x,y,z)=(x,x+z,z) projects onto U along span((0,1,0)).
items.proof_route: Compute P²=P, verify its range and kernel and the decomposition (x,y,z)=(x,x+z,z)+(0,y-x-z,0).

items.title: The indicators of {e}, {(12),(13),(23)}, {(123),(132)} form the class-function basis for S₃.
items.statement: The indicators of {e}, {(12),(13),(23)}, {(123),(132)} form the class-function basis for S₃.
items.proof_route: Verify the three orbits by the conjugation formula on transpositions and three-cycles; write f=f(e)1_e+f((12))1_transpositions+f((123))1_three-cycles and apply the A lemma.

references.title: Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory
Thomas W. Judson, Abstract Algebra: Theory and Applications

items.title: On X={1,2,3}, the normalized form has Gram matrix I₃/3 in the indicator basis. For f=(1,i,0) and h=(i,1,1), (f,h)=0 and (f,f)=2/3.
items.statement: On X={1,2,3}, the normalized form has Gram matrix I₃/3 in the indicator basis. For f=(1,i,0) and h=(i,1,1), (f,h)=0 and (f,f)=2/3.
items.proof_route: Compute each diagonal and off-diagonal basis pairing. Calculate (1·(-i)+i·1+0)/3=0 and (1+1)/3=2/3; sqrt(3) times each indicator gives an orthonormal basis.

references.title: Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition

items.title: The assertion that unit summands always attain the bound |sum z_i|=n is false: z_1=1,z_2=-1 give 0<2.
items.statement: The assertion that unit summands always attain the bound |sum z_i|=n is false: z_1=1,z_2=-1 give 0<2.
items.proof_route: Both summands have modulus one, their sum is zero, and the pairwise-difference identity gives 4-0=|1-(-1)|²=4.

references.title: Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory
